A Unifying View of Attention Sinks:
Two Algorithms, Two Solutions

Lukas Fesser ††thanks: Equal contribution and corresponding author.    Mozes Jacobs11footnotemark: 1    Thomas Fel11footnotemark: 1    Andy Keller    Sham Kakade Affiliation: Kempner Institute Affiliation: Harvard University Affiliation: Cambridge, MA Affiliation: {lukas_fesser, mozesjacobs, tfel}@g.harvard.edu
Abstract

When attention concentrates on a single token, a sink, what is the model actually computing? Attention sinks are ubiquitous in softmax transformers, yet this shared visual signature can hide fundamentally different algorithms. We show that visually similar sink patterns can reflect two distinct mechanisms: (i) adaptive  NOP** * From the NOP instruction in assembly. On many architectures, NOP is encoded as all zeros (unmapped memory returns zeroes by default), so a jump into the void does nothing gracefully. , where a head suppresses its update by routing to a null token, and (ii) broadcast, where a sink aggregates and redistributes global information. Proposed interventions like gating or registers work because they implicitly target one or the other, revealing a duality between method and assumed mechanism: gating implicitly assumes  NOP; registers implicitly assume broadcast. Each mechanism leaves distinct traces (NOP sinks exhibit negligible value norms; broadcast sinks induce low-rank outputs) which we formalize on synthetic tasks and use to derive practical diagnostics. Applied to pretrained vision transformers, these diagnostics reveal that both mechanisms exist at scale: sinks transition from CLS in early layers to patches in deeper layers, and concentrate in specialized heads. Strikingly, register tokens, designed for broadcast, are repurposed to also serve  NOP, confirming that neither intervention alone suffices. Combining gating with registers yields complementary gains in stability and performance.†† † Code available at: https://github.com/KempnerInstitute/attention_sink Overall, we find that the same attention pattern can reflect two very different computations and effective intervention requires first asking what the model is actually computing.

1 Introduction

Attention sinks – tokens that attract disproportionate attention mass across many queries – are pervasive in softmax transformers [1], especially vision transformers (ViTs) [2, 3, 4, 5] and large language models (LLMs) [6, 7, 8]. Empirically, they appear as near-vertical “stripes” in attention maps [9, 10, 11, 12], often at the [CLS] token or specific patch locations [13, 14, 15]. Yet the same visual signature can reflect very different computations, raising a practical question: when we see a sink, what algorithm is the model executing, and what intervention should we apply?

Related work has connected sink-like patterns to spectral concentration, rank collapse, anisotropy, massive activations, token-wise norm imbalance, and softmax saturation [16, 17, 11, 10, 12, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. These effects can harm stability and representation quality [23]. At the same time, sinks can be useful: in bidirectional attention, a token that aggregates and redistributes global information can act as a learned workspace [13]. Thus, “fixing” sinks in ViTs without understanding their role risks either removing useful computation or missing the source of instability.

The central challenge is that attention patterns alone are not mechanistic explanations [24, 25, 26]. A softmax head must place probability mass somewhere, so concentrating on a sink can mean either that the sink is informative or that it is a safe destination when the head should do nothing [27]. These cases can produce the same stripe: routing to a token with near-zero value norm implements an effective no-op (NOP) on the residual stream, while routing to a token with meaningful value broadcasts a shared component to many positions. Interventions designed for one mechanism may therefore fail when the other is active.

This perspective helps explain why the literature has not converged on a single mitigation. Gating mechanisms [28] and register tokens [13] both reduce sink-like behavior, but differ fundamentally in design and, under our view, target different computations rather than one shared pathology. What has been missing is a unified framing that separates these hypotheses, makes each identifiable in controlled settings, and yields diagnostics for determining which mechanism is operative in a given network, layer, or head. We take this step by treating sinks as arising from two computationally distinct algorithms—adaptive no-op (NOP) and broadcast—and by proposing measurable signatures based on both attention structure and residual-stream statistics.

Concretely, we develop a two-hypothesis view and connect each hypothesis to an intervention that targets it. Under Adaptive NOP, sinks suppress residual updates, predicting near-zero sink value norms and spectral/activation signatures of hard gating. Under Broadcast, sinks act as communication hubs, predicting non-negligible sink values, approximately low-rank attention outputs, and shared components across tokens. We instantiate both mechanisms with minimal synthetic objectives, use them to develop diagnostics, and apply the resulting tools to pretrained ViTs, where we find that both mechanisms co-occur. We further show that gated attention, which addresses NOP sinks, and register tokens, which support or regularize broadcast computation, provide complementary benefits. In summary, our contributions are the following:

  • •

    We show in controlled settings that visually similar sink patterns can implement distinct computations, and we derive diagnostics that distinguish NOP-like and broadcast-like sink behavior beyond what can be inferred from attention maps alone.

  • •

    We use these diagnostics to identify both regimes in pretrained ViTs, showing that they coexist within the same model across layers, heads, and register-equipped variants.

  • •

    We use this distinction to reinterpret sink mitigation, showing that gating and register tokens are complementary because they target different sink computations, and that combining them can yield stronger mitigation and improved downstream performance in settings where sink behavior matters.

2 Preliminaries and Related Work

2.1 Softmax Attention and Attention Sinks

We consider the attention mechanism of a Vision Transformer [2], which operates on a sequence of nn patch tokens with hidden representations 𝒙1,…,𝒙n∈ℝd\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Unlike autoregressive language models [28, 29, 7], ViTs employ bidirectional attention where each token can attend to all positions in the sequence. For a single attention head, treating individual token representations as column vectors, queries, keys, and values are computed as 𝒒i=𝑾Q⊤​𝒙i\bm{q}_{i}=\bm{W}_{Q}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}, 𝒌i=𝑾K⊤​𝒙i\bm{k}_{i}=\bm{W}_{K}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}, and 𝒗i=𝑾V⊤​𝒙i\bm{v}_{i}=\bm{W}_{V}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}, where 𝑾Q,𝑾K,𝑾V∈ℝd×dh\bm{W}_{Q},\bm{W}_{K},\bm{W}_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{h}} are learned projection matrices, so that 𝒒i,𝒌i,𝒗i∈ℝdh\bm{q}_{i},\bm{k}_{i},\bm{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}. We collect these column vectors into row-stacked matrices 𝑸,𝑲,𝑽∈ℝn×dh\bm{Q},\bm{K},\bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{h}} whose ii-th rows are 𝒒i⊤,𝒌i⊤,𝒗i⊤\bm{q}_{i}^{\top},\bm{k}_{i}^{\top},\bm{v}_{i}^{\top}, respectively. The single-head attention output at position ii is given by:

𝒐ihead=∑j=1n𝑨i​j​𝒗j,where​𝑨i​j=exp⁡(𝒒i⊤​𝒌j/dh)∑l=1nexp⁡(𝒒i⊤​𝒌l/dh).\bm{o}_{i}^{\mathrm{head}}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{ij}\bm{v}_{j},~~\text{where}~~{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{ij}=\frac{\exp(\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{k}_{j}/\sqrt{d_{h}})}{\sum_{l=1}^{n}\exp(\bm{q}_{i}^{\top}\bm{k}_{l}/\sqrt{d_{h}})}. (1)

Equivalently, in matrix form, the single-head output is 𝑶head=𝐀​𝑽∈ℝn×dh\bm{O}^{\mathrm{head}}=\mathbf{A}\bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{h}}, whose ii-th row is (𝒐ihead)⊤(\bm{o}_{i}^{\mathrm{head}})^{\top}.

The attention weights 𝑨i​j∈(0,1){\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{ij}\in(0,1) are bounded, and the attention matrix for all tokens 𝑨∈ℝn×n\bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is row-stochastic (forming a probability distribution over all nn positions for each query ii), thereby enabling information exchange within a single layer. We use the standard residual-stream convention: 𝒐iℓ∈ℝd\bm{o}_{i}^{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is added to 𝒙iℓ∈ℝd\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} as 𝒙iℓ+1=𝒙iℓ+𝒐iℓ\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell+1}=\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell}+\bm{o}_{i}^{\ell}, with other sublayers such as MLPs omitted here for clarity.

We now formally recall a central notion in our study: attention sinks. We define an attention sink (consistent with prior work [30, 31]) as a position that attracts disproportionate attention mass across many queries, without committing to a specific underlying cause.

Definition 1 (ϵ\epsilon-Attention Sink).

Let ϵ∈[0,1)\epsilon\in[0,1) be a small scalar. A position s∈{1,…,n}s\in\{1,\ldots,n\} is an ϵ\epsilon-attention sink with respect to a set of query indices ℐ⊆{1,…,n}\mathcal{I}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}, where by default ℐ={1,…,n}\mathcal{I}=\{1,\ldots,n\}, if, for all i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, the attention weight satisfies 𝐀i​s≥1−ϵ{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is}\geq 1-\epsilon.

ϵ=0\epsilon=0 corresponds to a perfect sink (all mass placed on ss), while smaller ϵ\epsilon indicates an approximately perfect sink (most mass on ss). To quantify sink behavior beyond a binary threshold, we use the (average) sink strength of a position ss over a query set ℐ\mathcal{I},

sink⁡(s,ℐ)=1|ℐ|​∑i∈ℐ𝑨i​s,\mathrm{sink}(s;\mathcal{I})\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is}, (2)

and we may refer to maxs⁡sink⁡(s,ℐ)\max_{s}\mathrm{sink}(s;\mathcal{I}) when measuring the strongest sink in a head. This classic definition (see [32] & [29]) captures the empirical phenomenon observed in vision transformers, where certain positions such as the [CLS] token or specific patch locations consistently attract high attention, while remaining agnostic to the mechanism producing this behavior.

2.2 Related Work

Attention sinks in LLMs.

Attention sinks have been studied extensively in autoregressive language models, where they often appear at early sequence positions or special tokens and can persist even when those positions are not semantically central [29, 9, 32, 31]. Prior work links this behavior to causal masking, long-context degradation, and architectural biases that make a small set of tokens convenient anchors for repeated attention [29, 28, 9, 33]. More recent analyses connect sink phenomena in LLMs to broader geometric and optimization effects, including spectral concentration, residual-stream imbalance, outlier activations, and dormant or conditionally inactive heads [10, 11, 18, 19, 20, 34]. This line of work has also motivated mitigation strategies such as gated attention and related attention modifications that reduce pathological concentration or allow heads to suppress their outputs more directly [20, 28]. Taken together, these papers establish that sink-like attention in LLMs is a robust and mechanistically meaningful phenomenon rather than a purely visual artifact.

Attention sinks in ViTs.

In vision transformers, sink-like patterns have been observed around the [CLS] token, specific patch locations, and learned workspace tokens such as registers [12, 13, 14, 22]. Existing work interprets these phenomena from several complementary perspectives. Some papers emphasize sinks as artifacts tied to outliers, saturation, or structured approximations in softmax attention [12, 20], while others argue that sink-like tokens can play a useful computational role by aggregating and redistributing global information [13]. Register-token methods are especially central in this literature, as they provide dedicated slots that absorb attention mass and often improve representation quality in pretrained ViTs [13, 14]. At the same time, recent analyses of ViT dynamics, rank collapse, oversmoothing, and position bias suggest that sink behavior is intertwined with broader questions about token mixing, representational diversity, and specialization across layers and heads [35, 36]. Overall, the ViT literature suggests that sink-like attention is related both to optimization pathologies and to potentially useful global coordination mechanisms, but does not yet provide a practical framework for distinguishing or mitigating these regimes when visually similar sink patterns appear within the same pretrained ViT.

3 Two Hypotheses for Attention Sinks

The signature of an attention sink (a vertical stripe in the attention map) is computationally ambiguous. Does the model attend to these tokens because they contain crucial information, or precisely because they do not? In this paper, we analyze two distinct computational regimes that can give rise to the same visual pattern. The goal of this section is not to provide a general theory of attention sinks, but to derive stylized mechanistic intuition and operational diagnostics that will later be applied to pretrained ViTs. We formally define these two regimes below, before analyzing their distinct spectral and geometric signatures in Sections 3.1 and 3.2. For simplicity, in the hypotheses below we use 𝒗s\bm{v}_{s} to denote the value contribution in the space being discussed: the single-head value in head-space analyses, and the output-projected value when referring to residual-stream updates.

Hypothesis 1 (Adaptive NOP).

An attention head implements an adaptive NOP mechanism [34, 29] if attention concentrates on a sink position ss. For tokens ii attending predominantly to ss, the output 𝐨i\bm{o}_{i} is negligible and the residual stream remains unchanged through the block, i.e. 𝐱iℓ+1≈𝐱iℓ\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell+1}\approx\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell}.

Hypothesis 2 (Broadcast).

An attention head implements a broadcast mechanism [13] if attention from many positions concentrates on a sink position ss whose value vector 𝐯s\bm{v}_{s} carries meaningful information. For tokens ii attending predominantly to ss, the residual stream update is dominated by the broadcast’s value: 𝐱iℓ+1−𝐱iℓ≈𝐀i​s​𝐯s\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell+1}-\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell}\approx{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is}\bm{v}_{s}. Consequently, the representations of tokens attending to ss acquire a shared linear component aligned with 𝐯s\bm{v}_{s}.

While both mechanisms produce similar attention patterns, they imply fundamentally different roles for the sink token and consequently require different interventions. Hypothesis 2 posits that the sink is not a passive operation for discarded attention mass, but an active component of the computation. In the following sections, we dissect them individually. We begin with the Adaptive NOP hypothesis.

3.1 Hypothesis 1: Sink as Adaptive NOP.

The first hypothesis posits that sinks arise when attention heads learn to selectively suppress their contribution to the residual stream. In transformers, attention outputs are added to the residual stream via 𝒙iℓ+1=𝒙iℓ+𝒐iℓ\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell+1}=\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell}+\bm{o}_{i}^{\ell}. When a head has no useful information to contribute for certain tokens, it must still produce an output due to the softmax normalization constraint [9]. Crucially, this behavior is adaptive: for some tokens the head performs a meaningful operation, while for others it routes to the sink and contributes nothing [34].

NOP Signatures.

Under this hypothesis, extreme attention logits and outlier activation norms are byproducts of the model learning to implement a null operation. The sink position serves as a learned null token that absorbs attention when no information transfer is needed. We may ask: is a negligible value norm the only way to achieve NOP behavior?

Lemma 1 (Uniqueness of NOP Solution).

Assume a single attention head with sink position ss and residual update 𝐨i=∑j𝐀i​j​𝐯j\bm{o}_{i}=\sum_{j}{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{ij}\bm{v}_{j}. For tokens ii routed predominantly to the sink, suppose the head implements an ϵ\epsilon-approximate NOP, i.e. ‖𝐨i‖≤ϵ\|\bm{o}_{i}\|\leq\epsilon. Then the no-op condition admits two solutions: the sink value 𝐯s\bm{v}_{s} can either (i) cancel out the residual contributions from other tokens, or (ii) have zero norm. As the sink becomes perfect (ϵ=0\epsilon=0), the cancellation mechanism vanishes, leaving ‖𝐯s‖=0\|\bm{v}_{s}\|=0 as the unique solution.

Having established the uniqueness of the NOP solution, we now address the adaptive nature of this function – that is, it must not perform a NOP permanently, but only when triggered. We examine the linear case (given the linearity of 𝑾Q\bm{W}_{Q} and 𝑾K\bm{W}_{K}) to understand how an attention head can function as a conditional gate. The attention probability 𝑨i​s{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is} must saturate to 11 specifically when a “flag” feature is detected. We show that this gating mechanism requires maximizing the query-key dot product, which can be achieved either through large activation norms at the sink position or through a dominant singular value in 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤\bm{W}_{Q}\bm{W}_{K}^{\top} aligned with the flag direction.

Lemma 2 (Mechanisms for Adaptivity).

Assume a linear query-key interaction with 𝐪i=𝐖Q⊤​𝐱i\bm{q}_{i}=\bm{W}_{Q}^{\top}\bm{x}_{i}, 𝐤s=𝐖K⊤​𝐱s\bm{k}_{s}=\bm{W}_{K}^{\top}\bm{x}_{s}, and interaction matrix 𝚯=𝐖Q​𝐖K⊤\bm{\Theta}=\bm{W}_{Q}\bm{W}_{K}^{\top}. To implement a hard gate (𝐀i​s=1{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is}=1) for specific queries, the pre-softmax logit Si​s=⟨𝐪i,𝐤s⟩/dhS_{is}=\langle\bm{q}_{i},\bm{k}_{s}\rangle/\sqrt{d_{h}} must significantly exceed competing logits. In this setting, the sink logit magnitude scales with ‖𝚯‖2⋅‖𝐱s‖\|\bm{\Theta}\|_{2}\cdot\|\bm{x}_{s}\|. Consequently, the model can implement gating via two regimes: (i) Spectral Gating: The interaction matrix 𝚯\bm{\Theta} learns a large leading singular value (spectral spike) aligned with the flag direction. (ii) Massive Activation: The sink token 𝐱s\bm{x}_{s} learns a disproportionately large norm, acting as a “super-attractor” or flag variable.

See Appendix B.1 for a constructive proof of both regimes. This duality could offer a theoretical explanation for the “massive activations” often observed in outlier tokens [13]: they might be the energetic cost of enforcing a reliable NOP gate without distorting the weights.

Toy Model of Adaptive NOP.

To isolate the mechanics of the adaptive NOP, we train a single-layer attention head on what could be summarized as a “conditional damping” task. The input is a sequence of tokens 𝒙i∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d)∈ℝd\bm{x}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The objective depends on the alignment between the token and a fixed gate vector 𝒗⋆\bm{v}^{\star}. If ⟨𝒙i,𝒗⋆⟩>0\langle\bm{x}_{i},\bm{v}^{\star}\rangle>0, the target is damped: 𝒚i=γ⋅𝒙i\bm{y}_{i}=\gamma\cdot\bm{x}_{i} (where γ=0\gamma=0 in the default experiment, is the NOP factor). Otherwise, the target preserves the input: 𝒚i=𝒙i\bm{y}_{i}=\bm{x}_{i}. The attention mechanism produces a convex combination of values (geometrically 𝒐⊆conv⁡(𝑽)\bm{o}\subseteq\mathrm{conv}(\bm{V})), so outputting ≈𝟎\approx\bm{0} for the positive-alignment tokens requires the head to use one of the two mechanisms explained in Lemma 2 (cancellation effect or null value vector). Conversely, to output 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} when ⟨𝒙i,𝒗⋆⟩<0\langle\bm{x}_{i},\bm{v}^{\star}\rangle<0, the head acts as an inductive head.

Results and Signatures.

We analyze the models trained on this toy model to understand how and why the NOP sinks emerge. We identify four key signatures of this mechanism: (i) SGD Optimization Converges to Sink Solutions. Our primary finding is that standard gradient descent consistently converges to a sink-based configuration to solve the adaptive NOP task. The complex dispersed attention pattern to cancel out contributions is not found by any model and the model consistently allocates a specific token ss to act as a null-reference. As shown in Figure 2A, the value vector 𝒗s\bm{v}_{s} at this position collapses to a near-zero norm, allowing the head to effectively “switch off” its output by routing the attention of flagged tokens to ss. (ii) Spectral Signature of Gating. The decision of when to route to the sink leaves a distinct trace in the weights. Figure 2B reveals that models with attention sinks exhibit a large dominant singular value in the interaction matrix 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤\bm{W}_{Q}\bm{W}_{K}^{\top}. As derived in Lemma 2, this spectral spike acts as a learned “flag detector,” amplifying the projection of specific tokens to saturate the softmax and force 𝑨i​s=1{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is}=1. We further study how sink solutions depend on the frequency/strength of the NOP condition (entropy and damping) in Appendix  A.1.

Summary.

The NOP hypothesis is a compelling explanation for one class of attention sinks. It suggests that these artifacts are the sign of a real algorithm: a dedicated zero token (‖𝒗s‖≈0||\bm{v}_{s}||\approx 0) coupled with a gating mechanism (high spectral norm or massive activation). This mechanism allows heads to be conditionally active, effectively solving the softmax constraint. However, this explains only sinks that suppress information. Do sinks ever propagate information? We now turn to our second hypothesis.

3.2 Hypothesis 2: Sink for Broadcasting.

Hypothesis 2 posits that sinks emerge from tokens that serve a functional role: aggregating global information and broadcasting it to other positions. In bidirectional attention, any token can gather information from and distribute it to all other tokens. A broadcast sink exploits this by accumulating a global representation and making it available sequence-wide.

Broadcast Signatures.

Under this hypothesis, high attention mass toward the sink reflects a meaningful computational pattern: the sink acts as a communication hub that distributes global or aggregated features across spatially distant patches. This leads to two measurable consequences. First, because the sink token’s value vector 𝒗s\bm{v}_{s} is added to many positions simultaneously, the resulting update matrix becomes low-rank.

Lemma 3 (Rank-1 update).

Suppose a single sink position ss dominates attention across many queries, so that the attention output satisfies 𝐎=𝐀​𝐕\bm{O}={\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}\bm{V} with 𝐀i​s≈1{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is}\approx 1 for those queries and 𝐯s\bm{v}_{s} carries non-negligible information. Then the output matrix 𝐎∈ℝn×dh\bm{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{h}} exhibits approximate rank-1 structure: 𝐎≈𝐀s​𝐯s⊤\bm{O}\approx{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{s}\bm{v}_{s}^{\top}.

Second, this repeated addition of the same vector 𝒗s\bm{v}_{s} to multiple tokens has a geometric effect on the latent space: it introduces a shared component across tokens, increasing their alignment.

Lemma 4 (Increased Token Similarity).

Suppose a broadcast sink at position ss dominates attention in a layer and let 𝐱¯ℓ=1n​∑i𝐱iℓ\bar{\bm{x}}^{\ell}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell} denote the mean token representation at layer ℓ\ell. Then the variance of token representations after a broadcast-dominated attention block satisfies:

1n∑i∥𝒙iℓ+1−𝒙¯ℓ+1∥2≤1n∑i\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\|\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell+1}-\bar{\bm{x}}^{\ell+1}\|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i} ‖𝒙iℓ−𝒙¯ℓ‖2+𝒪⁡(‖𝒗s‖2⋅𝕍⁡(𝑨s)).\displaystyle\|\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell}-\bar{\bm{x}}^{\ell}\|^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\|\bm{v}_{s}\|^{2}\cdot\mathbb{V}({\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{s})).

See Appendix B. This connects directly to recent findings by [35, 37, 36] regarding patch representations in standard ViTs that tend to converge toward their mean. Lemma 4 suggests that if this hypothesis holds, we should be able to induce sink behavior purely by forcing a model to solve a task requiring global information sharing.

Toy Model of Broadcasting.

To validate the broadcast hypothesis, we design a task that strictly requires global information sharing. We train a 2-layer Transformer on a “global broadcast” task (details in Appendix A.2). The input is a sequence of random tokens 𝒙i∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d)\bm{x}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\bm{I}_{d}).

The objective requires every token in the sequence to update its representation by adding a rotated version of this source token:

𝒚i=𝒙i+γ​𝑹​𝒙j⋆,\bm{y}_{i}=\bm{x}_{i}+\gamma\bm{R}\bm{x}_{j^{\star}}, (3)

where 𝑹∈ℝd×d\bm{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a fixed orthogonal rotation matrix and γ\gamma is a scalar controlling the broadcast strength. Unlike the NOP task, where the goal is to suppress updates, here the goal is to actively distribute specific information (𝒙j⋆\bm{x}_{j^{\star}}) from one position to all NN positions.

Results and Signatures.

We analyze the models trained on the Global Broadcast task to characterize the mechanisms of active information sharing. We identify four distinct signatures that we will now describe. (i) Emergence of Modular Broadcast Layers. While a multi-layer network could theoretically distribute the broadcasting operation across depth (e.g., partial mixing in every layer), we find that optimization consistently converges to a sharp, modular solution. As shown in Figure 3A, the model allocates a single layer to act as a dedicated broadcast (here, Layer 1) where attention concentrates entirely on the source token j∗j^{*}. The subsequent layer (Layer 2) defaults to an identity-like pattern (diagonal), preserving the broadcasted signal without further mixing. This suggests that sinks are not random artifacts, but represent stable, specialized algorithmic primitives that arise naturally under SGD for global communication. (ii) Information Transfer. A critical distinction from the NOP mechanism lies in the value vectors. Recall that NOP sinks suppress output by learning near-zero value norms. Here, Figure 3B shows that the distribution of value norms for sink tokens is indistinguishable from that of non-sink content tokens (both centered around ‖𝒗‖≈5.5\|\bm{v}\|\approx 5.5). This indicates the sink is actively writing a significant payload to the residual stream, consistent with Hypothesis 2. (iii) Geometry of Gating. The PCA projection of the Query-Key space (Figure 3C) reveals precisely how the model implements the conditional gating. First, all tokens collapse their query vectors into a one-dimensional query subspace (in the negative orthant of that subspace). Second, the selection is enforced via a double-negative alignment. The Sink Key (gold) is pushed deep into the negative half-space, aligning with the Universal Query (also negative) to produce a large positive logit. This collapse of queries and keys onto a single line implies that the interaction matrix 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤\bm{W}_{Q}\bm{W}_{K}^{\top} itself exhibits a sharp decay in singular values, effectively operating as a rank-1 projector that isolates the “broadcast” direction from all other feature dimensions. (iv) Low-Rank Updates. Finally, we validate the spectral signature predicted by Lemma 3. Figure 3D measures the stable rank [38, 39] of the attention update Sr⁡(𝒙iℓ+1−𝒙iℓ)\mathrm{Sr}(\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell+1}-\bm{x}_{i}^{\ell}) across layers. The broadcasting layer (Layer 1) exhibits a stable rank ≈1\approx 1, confirming that it is adding a single shared vector to the entire sequence. In contrast, the processing layer (Layer 2) maintains a higher effective rank, reflecting diverse, position-specific updates. We believe that this low-rank signature can serve as a robust diagnostic for detecting broadcast-like behavior in deep networks.

Two Algorithms, Two Signatures.

As elucidated by the preceding targeted analysis, the two algorithmic hypotheses for the role of attention sinks yield distinct measurable signatures in real models. Adaptive no-op sinks are characterized by negligible value norms at the sink position and representations that remain approximately unchanged through the attention block. Broadcast sinks, in contrast, exhibit non-zero value norms, induce low-rank structure in the attention output matrix, and increase cosine similarity across token representations as they distribute shared information. Taken together, these controlled analyses provide stylized support for the empirical story and yield operational diagnostics for distinguishing the two regimes. In the following section, we use these diagnostics to separate sink behavior in large-scale vision models and illuminate the role of attention sinks more broadly.

4 Empirical Evidence and Phenomenology

Having established the theoretical signatures of the Adaptive NOP and Broadcast mechanisms, we now examine their prevalence in large-scale Vision Transformers.

Phase Transition of Sink Tokens.

We investigate which tokens serve as sinks across layers and whether this varies by architecture. Figure 4 shows the attention inflow (the token receiving the highest attention mass per input) for DINOv2-L, DINOv2-G [40], and OpenCLIP-L-16 [41]. All three models exhibit a similar transition. In early layers, the [CLS] token acts as the primary sink. In deeper layers, this role shifts to patch tokens: [CLS] inflow decreases while patch sinks emerge. We now ask if sink behavior is distributed across all attention heads, or concentrated in specialized ones?

Head Specialization.

We map the frequency of sink behavior across layers and heads in DINOv2-L. Figure 5 reveals a sparse, vertical structure: certain heads act as sinks for nearly 80%80\% of inputs, while adjacent heads never do. This indicates that sink mechanisms are head specific. Given this specialization, we go back to our original main question: do these dedicated sink heads implement NOP, broadcast, or both?

Distinct Functional Regimes.

To answer this, we project every detected sink in DINOv2-G onto two diagnostic axes: the value norm ratio ‖𝒗s‖/‖𝒗i‖\|\bm{v}_{s}\|/\|\bm{v}_{i}\| and the stable rank of the attention update. Our main new empirical finding is not the existence of either regime in isolation, but that these regimes can be separated and shown to coexist within the same pretrained ViT. Figure 6 reveals two distinct modes.

The first cluster (early-to-mid layers) exhibits strongly suppressed value norms (<0.2×<0.2\times the baseline norm), consistent with Adaptive NOP: these heads nullify their contribution to the residual stream. The second cluster (deeper layers) shows standard value norms paired with strict rank-1 updates, consistent with Broadcast sink: these heads actively distribute shared information across the sequence. This dual phenomenology can also be found in other ViTs (see Appendix E). Finally, we study one of the most commonly used mitigation strategies for attention sinks in vision transformers – the addition of register tokens. Leveraging our new methodology, we thus ask: do registers fill the role of both mechanisms – or only one?

Validation via Registers.

We analyze DINOv2-G trained with 4 register tokens. If registers address sink behavior, they should absorb the attention mass currently forced onto patch tokens. Figure 8 (Left) confirms this: register tokens capture nearly all sink mass across layers, displacing both patch and [CLS] sinks. However, registers do not serve a single function. Figure 8 (Right) projects register sinks onto our diagnostic axes and reveals the same bimodal structure: a majority cluster with suppressed value norms (<0.2<0.2) implementing NOP, and a smaller cluster with ≈1\approx 1 norm and rank-1 updates implementing broadcast. This yields two insights. First, the “artifacts” in standard ViTs are genuine computational primitives – both NOP and broadcast persist even when dedicated tokens are provided. Second, while registers were designed with broadcasting in mind [13], the model repurposes them for NOP as well. This motivates the combination of registers with gating: registers provide a natural substrate for broadcasting, while gating offers a direct architectural implementation for NOP. We explore this in the next section.

5 Sink Mitigation Improves Dense Spatial Representations

This section explores the synergy between gated attention and register tokens together to mitigate attention sinks. We demonstrate empirically that these two methods are complementary; when combined, they produce better dense spatial representations than either technique used in isolation.

Experiments. We evaluate sink mitigation primarily in ViT-L LeJEPA models [42], whose latent-predictive objective encourages localized patch representations and is therefore well-suited for testing whether mitigation improves spatial features. We train three random seeds for each mitigation variant: a vanilla baseline, a model with four register tokens, a Gated Attention model (the ‘G1’ variant from Qiu et al. [28]), and a hybrid model combining Gated Attention with register tokens. For dense prediction, we freeze each trained backbone and train a single linear segmentation probe on ADE20K and Pascal VOC 2012. As a complementary classification control, we also report ImageNet-1k accuracy from online linear classifiers trained during LeJEPA pretraining. This allows us to compare whether sink mitigation improves patch-level spatial representations without necessarily improving global classification performance. Training configurations and hyperparameter settings are detailed in Appendix D.

Results. Table 1 shows that sink mitigation yields consistent gains on dense prediction tasks. The baseline achieves 0.166±0.0060.166\pm 0.006 on ADE20K and 0.438±0.0160.438\pm 0.016 on Pascal VOC 2012. All mitigation variants improve over this baseline on both datasets, indicating that reducing sink behavior improves spatial representations. Moreover, combining Gated Attention with register tokens yields the strongest performance, reaching 0.200±0.0060.200\pm 0.006 on ADE20K and 0.524±0.0130.524\pm 0.013 on Pascal VOC 2012. Consistent with these results, Figure 14 shows that both Gated Attention and register tokens reduce CLS and register token norms, with the combined variant also suppressing this sink-associated behavior.

By contrast, ImageNet-1k online linear classification accuracy remains tightly clustered across variants, with all models achieving approximately 69%69\% accuracy. This supports our interpretation: global classification depends primarily on aggregate image representations, whereas sink behavior mainly degrades localized patch-level features. Dense prediction tasks are therefore a more sensitive testbed for evaluating sink mitigation. Overall, these results suggest that Gated Attention and register tokens are complementary, with each improving dense prediction in isolation and their combination yielding the strongest spatial representations.

6 Discussion

This paper argues that attention sinks in vision transformers should not be treated as a single phenomenon: the same stripe-like attention pattern can implement different algorithms. We analyze two canonical mechanisms: Adaptive NOP, where a head routes attention to a sink to produce an approximately null residual update, and Broadcast, where a sink acts as a global workspace that aggregates and redistributes shared information. This framing yields simple diagnostics that connect attention maps to computation: sink value norms identify NOP-like suppression, while the rank structure of the attention-induced update identifies broadcast-like mixing. Minimal synthetic objectives isolate each mechanism, and applying these diagnostics to pretrained ViTs suggests that both occur in practice, with register-like tokens often shifting where sink behavior concentrates rather than uniformly eliminating it. Empirically, combining gating and registers eliminates NOP sinks, redirects broadcast sinks to registers, and improves dense prediction: ImageNet classification remains largely unchanged, while ADE20K and Pascal VOC 2012 linear probes improve across mitigation variants, with gating + registers performing best. This supports the view that sink mitigation primarily improves patch-level spatial representations rather than global classification accuracy.

Our analysis also has limitations and points to concrete next steps. First, although gated attention improves training dynamics in LLMs [28], it remains unclear when analogous benefits arise in ViTs, especially because gated attention and registers do not remove broadcast sinks. Our LeJEPA results suggest that benefits may be clearest when localized patch representations matter, but future work should test whether they persist or grow with model, data, and training scale. Controlled studies should track update norms, sharpness, downstream spatial performance, and the emergence timing of sink-like heads under gating and registers. Second, if some sinks are useful broadcasters, can architecture support broadcasting without inducing sink behavior? More broadly, linking attention computations to the architectural constraints that encourage them may help redesign attention to preserve what helps learning while removing what hinders it.

Appendix A Toy Models of Attention Sinks

A.1 Toy Model of NOP

We implement the NOP task from section 3.1 using a deliberately minimal single-head Transformer block (no MLP) that mirrors a ViT attention layer with pre-norm residual. Each forward pass applies LayerNorm to the token stream, forms 𝑸,𝑲,𝑽\bm{Q},\bm{K},\bm{V} with learned linear maps (no bias), and computes attention weights 𝑨=softmax⁡(𝐐𝐊⊤/dh)∈ℝL×L{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}=\softmax(\bm{Q}\bm{K}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{h}})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L}; the attention branch produces a residual update Δ​𝑶=𝑾O​(𝑨​𝑽)\Delta\bm{O}=\bm{W}_{O}({\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}\bm{V}), and the block output is 𝑶=𝐗+Δ​𝑶\bm{O}=\mathbf{X}+\Delta\bm{O}, where 𝐗\mathbf{X} denotes the normalized and position-embedded stream used to form 𝑸,𝑲,𝑽\bm{Q},\bm{K},\bm{V}. We use model width d=64d=64, head dimension dh=64d_{h}=64, and sequence length L=32L=32, with learned positional embeddings and a learned BOS offset added to token 00 prior to LayerNorm. Training data are i.i.d. Gaussian token sequences 𝐗in∈ℝB×L×d\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times d} sampled fresh each step. To define the NOP mask, we sample once a fixed unit vector 𝒗∈ℝd\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (no gradients) and compute scores si=⟨(𝐗in)i,𝒗⟩s_{i}=\langle(\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{in}})_{i},\bm{v}\rangle per token; the mask is 𝐦i=𝟙[si>λ]\mathbf{m}_{i}=\mathbbm{1}[s_{i}>\lambda]. The regression target is imposed on the attention branch,

Δ​𝒚i=(1−𝐦i)​(𝐗in)i+𝐦i​γ​(𝐗in)i,\Delta\bm{y}_{i}=(1-\mathbf{m}_{i})\,(\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{in}})_{i}\;+\;\mathbf{m}_{i}\,\gamma\,(\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{in}})_{i},

so that γ=0\gamma=0 enforces a true NOP condition for the attention head (masked tokens should produce zero residual update, leaving the residual stream unchanged), while γ>0\gamma>0 makes the task “partially damped” rather than fully nulled. We optimize mean-squared error ‖Δ​𝑶−Δ​𝐘‖22\|\Delta\bm{O}-\Delta\mathbf{Y}\|_{2}^{2} with AdamW (learning rate 3⋅10−33\cdot 10^{-3}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}), typically for 30k steps at batch size B=1024B=1024 (or B=2048B=2048 for sweep runs), on GPU.

To measure sink emergence during training we track a simple sink score computed from the average attention mass per key position: for a batch attention tensor 𝑨∈ℝB×L×L{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times L} we form a¯j=1B​L​∑b,i𝑨b​i​j\bar{a}_{j}=\frac{1}{BL}\sum_{b,i}{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{bij} (average attention received by position jj), and report maxj⁡a¯j\max_{j}\bar{a}_{j} as the sink score (with stdj​(a¯j)\mathrm{std}_{j}(\bar{a}_{j}) used for uncertainty bands). We log this quantity every 10 steps and visualize its evolution versus training steps. Two sweeps used in Figure 3 are implemented as follows: (i) a damping sweep over γ∈{0,10−3,10−2,10−1,0.5,1.0}\gamma\in\{0,10^{-3},10^{-2},10^{-1},0.5,1.0\}, holding λ=0\lambda=0 fixed (so ℙ[𝐦i=1]≈0.5\mathbb{P}[\mathbf{m}_{i}=1]\approx 0.5 under Gaussian inputs), and (ii) an activation-frequency sweep over thresholds λ\lambda chosen to realize target no-op probabilities in [0.1,0.9][0.1,0.9] via the standard-normal tail mapping λ=Φ−1​(1−p)\lambda=\Phi^{-1}(1-p). Finally, to connect sinks to the interaction spectrum, we train one “sink” model (λ=0\lambda=0) and one “no-sink” baseline (λ=10\lambda=10) for 10k steps and compare the singular values of the induced query–key interaction matrix 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤∈ℝdh×dh\bm{W}_{Q}\bm{W}_{K}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times d_{h}} (computed by SVD on 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤\bm{W}_{Q}\bm{W}_{K}^{\top}), reproducing the sharp spectral spike associated with the sink solution.

A.1.1 Optimization sweeps: entropy and damping

(i) High Entropy Accelerates Emergence. We investigate whether the frequency of the NOP condition in the dataset affects sink formation. We find that entropy of NOP existence impacts the number of iterations to find a sink: the sink solution emerges most rapidly when the model faces maximum entropy (50% probability of NOP) as seen in Figure 7A. Crucially, however, the mechanism is robust to low-entropy settings; even when the NOP condition is rare, the sink topology still eventually emerges, though it requires more optimization steps to settle.

(ii) Damping is Sufficient (Strict Zero Not Required). Finally, we test if a strict zero-output constraint is necessary to trigger this phenomenon. We relax the objective to merely dampen the signal (setting the target 𝒚i=0.1⋅𝒙i\bm{y}_{i}=0.1\cdot\bm{x}_{i} instead of 𝟎\bm{0}). We find that partial damping is sufficient: the optimization pressure to reduce the norm of the residual update acts as a strong enough incentive for the model to allocate a dedicated sink token, rather than attempting to dampen the signal via distributed attention (Figure 7B). To put it simply, even an approximate NOP task is enough to make the sinks appear.

A.2 Toy Model of Broadcast

We implement the broadcast task of Eq. (6) using a minimal 2-layer ViT-style block with one attention head per layer and pre-norm residual structure. Concretely, each attention layer applies LayerNorm, computes 𝑸,𝑲,𝑽\bm{Q},\bm{K},\bm{V} via linear maps (no bias) to a head dimension equal to the model width (d=dh=64d=d_{h}=64), forms 𝑨=softmax⁡(𝐐𝐊⊤/dh)∈ℝL×L{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}=\softmax(\bm{Q}\bm{K}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{h}})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L}, and writes back through a linear output map with a residual on the original stream (i.e., 𝐗out=𝐗in+𝑾O​(𝑨​𝑽)\mathbf{X}_{\text{out}}=\mathbf{X}_{\text{in}}+\bm{W}_{O}({\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}\bm{V})). Each layer is followed by an MLP block LN→Linear​(d,4​d)→GELU→Linear​(4​d,d)\text{LN}\rightarrow\text{Linear}(d,4d)\rightarrow\text{GELU}\rightarrow\text{Linear}(4d,d) with a residual. We use sequence length L=32L=32, learned positional embeddings added only in the first attention layer, and train on i.i.d. Gaussian token sequences 𝐗∈ℝB×L×d\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times d} with batch size B=1024B=1024 on GPU. The selector direction 𝒖\bm{u} is sampled once and fixed, and the rotation 𝐑\mathbf{R} is sampled once as an (approximately) orthogonal matrix via QR factorization. Training minimizes mean-squared error between model outputs and the broadcast targets (Eq. (6)) using AdamW for 30k steps (learning rate 5⋅10−45\cdot 10^{-4}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}), with broadcast strength α\alpha typically set to 1.01.0.

To quantify whether attention implements a broadcast hub, we track (i) sink matching: for each sample, we predict a sink index ȷ^\hat{\jmath} by taking the dominant column of attention mass, ȷ^=arg⁡maxj​1L​∑i𝑨i​j\hat{\jmath}=\arg\max_{j}\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i}{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{ij}, and report the fraction of matches to the ground-truth selected index j⋆j^{\star} (as well as the corresponding peak column mass as a “sink strength”). We also measure mechanistic correlates available from the forward pass: norms of the values and keys at the selected token, ‖𝒗j⋆‖\|\bm{v}_{j^{\star}}\| and ‖𝒌j⋆‖\|\bm{k}_{j^{\star}}\|, compared to average ‖𝒗‖\|\bm{v}\| and ‖𝒌‖\|\bm{k}\| across positions; the per-token magnitude of the pre-output update ‖(𝑨​𝑽)t‖\|({\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}\bm{V})_{t}\| (reporting mean and standard deviation across tt as a proxy for how uniformly the payload is written across the sequence); and the similarity structure of queries across positions via cosine similarity to a reference query (e.g. 𝒒0\bm{q}_{0}). These diagnostics are used to distinguish how the model routes attention to the selected token (e.g. amplifying ‖𝒌j⋆‖\|\bm{k}_{j^{\star}}\| versus making queries near-constant for easy alignment) and to verify that the induced update is contentful and broadly distributed, consistent with the broadcast mechanism.

Appendix B Two Hypotheses for Attention Sinks

We start by recalling our definition of a sink:

Definition 2 (ϵ\epsilon-Sink).

A position ss is an ϵ\epsilon-sink if 𝐀i​s≥1−ϵ{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is}\geq 1-\epsilon for all positions i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, where ϵ∈[0,1)\epsilon\in[0,1) is small.

B.1 Proof of Lemma 2: Mechanisms of Adaptivity

Proof.

Consider a simplified attention mechanism with a single head. Let 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} be a query token and 𝒙s\bm{x}_{s} be the dedicated sink token. The attention score (logit) for the sink is given by:

Si​s=1dh​𝒙i⊤​𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤​𝒙s=1dh​𝒙i⊤​𝚯​𝒙s.S_{is}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\bm{W}_{Q}\bm{W}_{K}^{\top}\bm{x}_{s}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\Theta}\bm{x}_{s}. (4)

We assume the gating decision is based on a specific feature direction 𝒖\bm{u} (with ‖𝒖‖=1\|\bm{u}\|=1). We decompose the query as 𝒙i=λi​𝒖+𝒙⟂\bm{x}_{i}=\lambda_{i}\bm{u}+\bm{x}_{\perp}, where λi\lambda_{i} is the scalar activation of the feature triggering the NOP, and 𝒙⟂⟂𝒖\bm{x}_{\perp}\perp\bm{u}.

To consistently route attention to the sink when the feature is active (λi>0\lambda_{i}>0), the model aligns the interaction matrix 𝚯\bm{\Theta} and the sink token 𝒙s\bm{x}_{s} with this direction. We construct:

  • •

    The interaction matrix as rank-1: 𝚯=σ​𝒖​𝒖⊤\bm{\Theta}=\sigma\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top}, where σ=‖𝚯‖2\sigma=\|\bm{\Theta}\|_{2} is the spectral norm.

  • •

    The sink token as aligned with the flag: 𝒙s=γs​𝒖\bm{x}_{s}=\gamma_{s}\bm{u}, where γs=‖𝒙s‖\gamma_{s}=\|\bm{x}_{s}\| is the token norm.

Substituting these into the attention score equation:

Si​s=1dh​(λi​𝒖+𝒙⟂)⊤​(σ​𝒖​𝒖⊤)​(γs​𝒖)=λi​σ​γsdh.S_{is}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}(\lambda_{i}\bm{u}+\bm{x}_{\perp})^{\top}(\sigma\bm{u}\bm{u}^{\top})(\gamma_{s}\bm{u})=\frac{\lambda_{i}\sigma\gamma_{s}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}. (5)

For the attention weight 𝑨i​s{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is} to approach 1 (hard gating), the score Si​sS_{is} must exceed the scores of all other NN tokens by a large margin MM (where MM depends on the desired sharpness of the softmax). That is:

λi​σ​γsdh≫maxj≠s⁡Si​j⟹σ​γs≫M​dhλi.\frac{\lambda_{i}\sigma\gamma_{s}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\gg\max_{j\neq s}S_{ij}\implies\sigma\gamma_{s}\gg\frac{M\sqrt{d_{h}}}{\lambda_{i}}. (6)

This inequality σ​γs≫C\sigma\gamma_{s}\gg C reveals the two distinct optimization paths available to the model to satisfy the gating condition: (i) Spectral Gating: The model increases σ\sigma (the singular value of 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤\bm{W}_{Q}\bm{W}_{K}^{\top}) while keeping the sink norm γs\gamma_{s} moderate. (ii) Massive Activation: The model increases γs\gamma_{s} (the norm of the sink token 𝒙s\bm{x}_{s}) while keeping the weight spectral norm σ\sigma moderate. Both solutions are mathematically equivalent for producing the necessary logit Si​sS_{is} to trigger the sink. ∎

B.2 Adaptive No-Op

Lemma 5 (Uniqueness of No-Op Solution).

Let ss be an ϵ\epsilon-sink and suppose the no-op constraint ‖𝐨i‖≤δ\|\bm{o}_{i}\|\leq\delta holds for all tokens ii. Let Vmax=maxj⁡‖𝐯j‖V_{\max}=\max_{j}\|\bm{v}_{j}\|. When ϵ>0\epsilon>0, two solutions satisfy this constraint: either the sink has negligible value norm ‖𝐯s‖≤δ+ϵ⋅Vmax\|\bm{v}_{s}\|\leq\delta+\epsilon\cdot V_{\max}, or the sink’s value vector cancels the residual contribution from other tokens. However, as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, the cancellation solution vanishes and ‖𝐯s‖≤δ\|\bm{v}_{s}\|\leq\delta becomes the unique solution.

Proof.

Let ss be an ϵ\epsilon-sink. The attention output for any token ii is:

𝒐i=𝑨i​s​𝒗s+∑j≠s𝑨i​j​𝒗j=(1−ϵi)​𝒗s+𝒓i,\bm{o}_{i}={\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is}\bm{v}_{s}+\sum_{j\neq s}{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{ij}\bm{v}_{j}=(1-\epsilon_{i})\bm{v}_{s}+\bm{r}_{i}, (7)

where ϵi=1−𝑨i​s≤ϵ\epsilon_{i}=1-{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{is}\leq\epsilon and the residual 𝒓i=∑j≠s𝑨i​j​𝒗j\bm{r}_{i}=\sum_{j\neq s}{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{ij}\bm{v}_{j} satisfies ‖𝒓i‖≤ϵ⋅Vmax\|\bm{r}_{i}\|\leq\epsilon\cdot V_{\max}.

When ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the constraint ‖𝒐i‖≤δ\|\bm{o}_{i}\|\leq\delta admits two types of solutions. The first sets ‖𝒗s‖≈0\|\bm{v}_{s}\|\approx 0, yielding ‖𝒐i‖≈‖𝒓i‖≤ϵ⋅Vmax\|\bm{o}_{i}\|\approx\|\bm{r}_{i}\|\leq\epsilon\cdot V_{\max}. The second exploits cancellation by choosing 𝒗s≈−𝒓i/(1−ϵi)\bm{v}_{s}\approx-\bm{r}_{i}/(1-\epsilon_{i}), yielding 𝒐i≈𝟎\bm{o}_{i}\approx\bm{0}.

As ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, the residual vanishes: 𝒓i→𝟎\bm{r}_{i}\to\bm{0}. The output simplifies to 𝒐i→𝒗s\bm{o}_{i}\to\bm{v}_{s}, so the constraint ‖𝒐i‖≤δ\|\bm{o}_{i}\|\leq\delta becomes ‖𝒗s‖≤δ\|\bm{v}_{s}\|\leq\delta. The cancellation solution also converges to 𝒗s→𝟎\bm{v}_{s}\to\bm{0} since there is nothing left to cancel. Thus ‖𝒗s‖≈0\|\bm{v}_{s}\|\approx 0 is the unique solution in this limit. ∎

Proof of Corollary 3.

𝑨=𝑨s​𝒆s⊤+𝑬,{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}={\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{s}\bm{e}_{s}^{\top}+\bm{E}, (8)

Appendix C Extended Literature Review

C.1 Gated Attention

We briefly describe the gated attention modification of softmax attention [28] used throughout this paper. Starting from the standard single-head formulation in Eq. (1), let 𝐗∈ℝn×d\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} denote the matrix whose ii-th row is 𝒙i⊤\bm{x}_{i}^{\top}, and let

𝑸=𝐗​𝑾Q,𝑲=𝐗​𝑾K,𝑽=𝐗​𝑾V,\bm{Q}=\mathbf{X}\bm{W}_{Q},\quad\bm{K}=\mathbf{X}\bm{W}_{K},\quad\bm{V}=\mathbf{X}\bm{W}_{V}, (22)
𝐒=𝑸​𝑲⊤dh,𝑨=softmax⁡(𝐒),𝐎=𝐀​𝐕.\mathbf{S}=\frac{\bm{Q}\bm{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}},\quad{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}=\softmax(\mathbf{S}),\quad\bm{O}={\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}\bm{V}. (23)

Gated attention introduces an additional gate computed from a (typically pre-normalized) hidden-state signal and uses it to modulate one of the intermediate quantities in the attention block. In its generic (multiplicative) form, given an input 𝐘\mathbf{Y} to be gated and a signal 𝐗\mathbf{X} from which to compute gate scores, we define

g⁡(𝐘,𝐗):=𝐘⊙σ⁡(𝐗​𝑾θ),g(\mathbf{Y};\mathbf{X})\;:=\;\mathbf{Y}\odot\sigma(\mathbf{X}\bm{W}_{\theta}), (24)

where 𝑾θ\bm{W}_{\theta} are learnable parameters, σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is an activation function (by default a sigmoid), and ⊙\odot denotes elementwise multiplication.

Default gated-softmax output.

Unless stated otherwise, we use head-specific, multiplicative sigmoid gating applied to the SDPA (softmax-attention) output. Concretely, for a single head we compute a gate matrix

𝐆=σ⁡(𝐗​𝑾θ)∈ℝn×dh,\mathbf{G}\;=\;\sigma(\mathbf{X}\bm{W}_{\theta})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{h}}, (25)

and form the gated head output

𝑶~=𝑶⊙𝐆=(𝑨​𝑽)⊙σ⁡(𝐗​𝑾θ),\widetilde{\bm{O}}\;=\;\bm{O}\odot\mathbf{G}\;=\;({\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}\bm{V})\odot\sigma(\mathbf{X}\bm{W}_{\theta}), (26)

i.e 𝒐~i=𝒐i⊙σ⁡(𝒙i​𝑾θ)\widetilde{\bm{o}}_{i}\;=\;\bm{o}_{i}\odot\sigma(\bm{x}_{i}\bm{W}_{\theta}). This 𝒐~i\widetilde{\bm{o}}_{i} then replaces 𝒐i\bm{o}_{i} in the residual update. One can analogously gate other locations (e.g., 𝑸\bm{Q}, 𝑲\bm{K}, 𝑽\bm{V}, or the concatenated multi-head output); when relevant, we will specify the gated quantity explicitly while keeping the same notation as above.

C.2 Register Tokens

We also consider the register token modification of a ViT [13], which appends a small number of additional learnable tokens to the input sequence. Concretely, let 𝒙1,…,𝒙n∈ℝd\bm{x}_{1},\dots,\bm{x}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the patch-token representations (and optionally a class token, treated as an additional special token in the same way). We introduce rr register tokens with learnable embeddings 𝒓1,…,𝒓r∈ℝd\bm{r}_{1},\dots,\bm{r}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that are independent of the input image and are appended to the sequence after patch embedding. The resulting extended sequence has length n~=n+r\tilde{n}=n+r and can be written as

𝐗~=[𝒙1⊤𝒙n⊤𝒓1⊤𝒓r⊤]∈ℝn~×d,\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\;=\;\begin{bmatrix}\bm{x}_{1}^{\top}\\[-2.0pt] \vdots\\[-2.0pt] \bm{x}_{n}^{\top}\\[-2.0pt] \bm{r}_{1}^{\top}\\[-2.0pt] \vdots\\[-2.0pt] \bm{r}_{r}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{\tilde{n}\times d}, (27)

with n~=n+r\tilde{n}=n+r. Attention is then computed without any other change on 𝐗~\tilde{\mathbf{X}}: for each head,

𝑸~=𝐗~​𝑾Q,𝑲~=𝐗~​𝑾K,𝑽~=𝐗~​𝑾V,\tilde{\bm{Q}}=\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\bm{W}_{Q},\quad\tilde{\bm{K}}=\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\bm{W}_{K},\quad\tilde{\bm{V}}=\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\bm{W}_{V},\quad (28)
𝐒~=𝑸~​𝑲~⊤dh,𝑨~=softmax⁡(𝐒~),𝐎~=𝐀~​𝐕~.\tilde{\mathbf{S}}=\frac{\tilde{\bm{Q}}\tilde{\bm{K}}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}},\quad\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}}=\softmax(\tilde{\mathbf{S}}),\quad\tilde{\bm{O}}=\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}}\tilde{\bm{V}}. (29)

The same residual update is applied to all n~\tilde{n} tokens. At the end of the network, the register tokens are discarded: downstream representations use only the original tokens (e.g., patch tokens and optionally [CLS]), while registers serve purely as internal workspace during the forward pass.

C.3 Non-softmax Attention

1. Clipped-softmax attention.

Clipped-softmax [20] replaces the usual row-wise softmax with a stretched-and-clipped variant. First form standard softmax weights

𝑨~=softmax⁡(𝐒)∈ℝn×n,a~i​j=esi​j∑k=1nesi​k.\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}}=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{S})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\quad\tilde{a}_{ij}=\frac{e^{s_{ij}}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}e^{s_{ik}}}. (30)

Given hyperparameters ζ≥1\zeta\geq 1, γ≤0\gamma\leq 0, define the elementwise clipped-softmax

clipped​_​softmax⁡(𝐒,ζ,γ):=clip⁡((ζ−γ)​𝑨~+γ, 0,1),\operatorname{clipped\_softmax}(\mathbf{S};\zeta,\gamma):=\operatorname{clip}\big((\zeta-\gamma)\,\tilde{{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}}+\gamma,\;0,1\big), (31)

where clip⁡(x,0,1)\operatorname{clip}(x,0,1) truncates each entry to [0,1][0,1]. The attention matrix is

𝑨clip=clipped​_​softmax⁡(𝐒,ζ,γ),Attnclip⁡(𝐗)=𝑨clip​𝑽.{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{clip}}=\operatorname{clipped\_softmax}(\mathbf{S};\zeta,\gamma),\quad\operatorname{Attn}_{\text{clip}}(\mathbf{X})={\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{clip}}\bm{V}. (32)

Softmax outputs in (0,1)(0,1) are stretched to (γ,ζ)(\gamma,\zeta) and then clipped back to [0,1][0,1], so entries larger than 1−γζ−γ\tfrac{1-\gamma}{\zeta-\gamma} become exactly 11 and entries smaller than −γζ−γ-\tfrac{\gamma}{\zeta-\gamma} become exactly 00. This allows exact zeros/ones with finite score ranges and kills gradients where clipping is active.

2. ReLU-attention with 1/n1/n sequence-length scaling.

ReLU-attention [43] uses a pointwise ReLU on scores and normalizes only by sequence length. For each pair (i,j)(i,j),

ai​jReLU=1n​ReLU⁡(si​j)=1n​max⁡{si​j,0},a_{ij}^{\text{ReLU}}=\frac{1}{n}\,\operatorname{ReLU}(s_{ij})=\frac{1}{n}\,\max\{s_{ij},0\}, (33)

so the attention matrix is

𝑨ReLU=1n​ReLU⁡(𝐒)(elementwise).{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{ReLU}}=\frac{1}{n}\,\operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf{S})\quad\text{(elementwise)}. (34)

The output is

AttnReLU⁡(𝐗)=𝑨ReLU​𝑽=1n​ReLU⁡(𝐒)​𝑽.\operatorname{Attn}_{\text{ReLU}}(\mathbf{X})={\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{ReLU}}\bm{V}=\frac{1}{n}\,\operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf{S})\,\bm{V}. (35)

Rows of 𝑨ReLU{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{ReLU}} are not normalized to sum to 11; the factor 1/n1/n is chosen so that at (random) initialization 𝔼j​[ai​jReLU]=O⁡(1/n)\mathbb{E}_{j}[a_{ij}^{\text{ReLU}}]=O(1/n), matching the scale of standard softmax attention without requiring a reduction over the sequence dimension.

3. General scaled point-wise attention family.

This family generalizes ReLU-attention by replacing softmax with a generic elementwise nonlinearity plus a length-dependent scaling [44]. For an activation h:ℝ→ℝh:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} and exponent α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], define

ai​j(h,α)=n−α​h​(si​j),𝑨h,α=n−α​h​(𝐒)​(elementwise).a_{ij}^{(h,\alpha)}=n^{-\alpha}\,h(s_{ij}),\quad{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{h,\alpha}=n^{-\alpha}h(\mathbf{S})\;\;\text{(elementwise)}. (36)

The attention output is

Attnh,α⁡(𝐗)=𝑨h,α​𝑽=n−α​h​(𝐒)​𝑽,\operatorname{Attn}_{h,\alpha}(\mathbf{X})={\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{h,\alpha}\bm{V}=n^{-\alpha}h(\mathbf{S})\bm{V}, (37)

with hh chosen from ReLU\operatorname{ReLU}, ReLU2\operatorname{ReLU}^{2}, GELU\operatorname{GELU}, softplus\operatorname{softplus}, identity, sigmoid\operatorname{sigmoid}. ReLU-attention is recovered as the special case h=ReLUh=\operatorname{ReLU}, α=1\alpha=1. Empirically, α≈1\alpha\approx 1 stabilizes training by keeping the typical magnitude of entries ai​j(h,α)a_{ij}^{(h,\alpha)} on the order of 1/n1/n, again echoing the effective scaling provided by softmax.

4. Polynomial attention with 1/n\sqrt{1/n} scaling.

Polynomial attention [44] replaces the softmax by an elementwise polynomial of the scores, with a 1/n\sqrt{1/n} prefactor chosen to control the Frobenius norm of the attention matrix. Starting from the same score matrix 𝐒\mathbf{S}, define for a degree-p>0p>0 power

𝑨poly=1n​𝐒⊙p,{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{poly}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}\,\mathbf{S}^{\odot p}, (38)

where 𝐒⊙p\mathbf{S}^{\odot p} denotes the elementwise power (𝐒⊙p)i​j=si​jp(\mathbf{S}^{\odot p})_{ij}=s_{ij}^{p}. The head output is

Attnpoly⁡(𝐗)=𝑨poly​𝑽=1n​𝐒⊙p​𝑽.\operatorname{Attn}_{\text{poly}}(\mathbf{X})={\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{poly}}\bm{V}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}\,\mathbf{S}^{\odot p}\bm{V}. (39)

In the experiments they focus on cubic activations, e.g. φ⁡(x)=1k​x3\varphi(x)=\tfrac{1}{k}x^{3} with k≈nk\approx\sqrt{n} (fixed or learned “dynamic scale”), which fits this template up to a constant factor. Under Gaussian assumptions on 𝑸,𝑲\bm{Q},\bm{K}, the 1/n\sqrt{1/n} scaling yields ‖𝑨poly‖F=O⁡(n)\|{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{poly}}\|_{F}=O(\sqrt{n}) and similarly controlled Jacobians, mimicking softmax’s implicit Frobenius-norm regularization while dropping non-negativity, normalization, and sparsity.

5. Sigmoid self-attention.

Sigmoid attention [45] replaces row-wise softmax by an elementwise sigmoid with an additive bias that can depend on nn. With the same 𝐒\mathbf{S}, define

σb​(u):=(1+e−(u+b))−1\sigma_{b}(u):=\bigl(1+e^{-(u+b)}\bigr)^{-1} (40)

for a learnable or hand-chosen bias bb (scalar or matrix). Then

𝑨sig=σb​(𝐒)(elementwise),ai​jsig=σ⁡(si​j+b),{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{sig}}=\sigma_{b}(\mathbf{S})\quad\text{(elementwise)},\qquad a_{ij}^{\text{sig}}=\sigma\bigl(s_{ij}+b\bigr), (41)

and

Attnsig⁡(𝐗)=𝑨sig​𝑽=σb​(𝐒)​𝑽.\operatorname{Attn}_{\text{sig}}(\mathbf{X})={\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{sig}}\bm{V}=\sigma_{b}(\mathbf{S})\,\bm{V}. (42)

Rows of 𝑨sig{\color[rgb]{0.0313,0.5703,0.6992}\bm{A}}_{\text{sig}} are not normalized and entries lie strictly in (0,1)(0,1). With appropriate normalization schemes and a suitable choice of bb (often roughly b≈−log⁡nb\approx-\log n at initialization), attention norms remain controlled, and SigmoidAttn-based transformers can act as universal approximators with different regularity properties compared to softmax attention, while remaining compatible with efficient kernels such as FLASH-SIGMOID.

C.4 Other Related Works

Attention sinks in LLMs.

In autoregressive LLMs, attention sinks often coincide with special tokens (e.g., beginning-of-sequence), high-frequency separators (newlines, punctuation), or early positions that become convenient aggregation points under causal masking [33]. Once established, sinks can reduce the model’s effective context utilization: instead of distributing attention to the most relevant evidence, a significant fraction of attention is repeatedly spent on a small set of sink positions, which can manifest as degraded long-context retrieval, increased copying of boilerplate, or brittle reasoning when relevant operands are far apart in the prompt [9, 28]. This behavior is particularly salient in settings where the model must integrate multiple dispersed constraints—precisely the regime emphasized by our relational reasoning perspective—because sink formation can act like an implicit bottleneck that prioritizes globally “easy-to-attend” anchors over the specific relational evidence needed for correct composition.

Mitigation strategies beyond register tokens and gated attention.

Beyond architectural additions like register tokens and modifications like gated attention, sinks can be mitigated via (i) normalization and scaling interventions that prevent extreme QK logits (e.g., QK-normalization, per-head temperature control, or logit clipping) so that a small set of keys cannot dominate attention across many queries; (ii) regularization objectives that discourage overly peaky or position-collapsed attention patterns (e.g., entropy/coverage penalties, auxiliary losses that promote diversity across heads, or discouraging persistent mass on special-token keys); (iii) data and curriculum strategies, such as training on longer contexts with targeted supervision requiring evidence far from the prompt prefix (and augmentations that randomize separators/formatting), which reduces the incentive to overuse early “anchor” tokens; and (iv) inference-time adjustments, including attention temperature tuning, selective head masking/pruning for sink-heavy heads, or KV-cache compression policies that preserve high-utility keys while downweighting persistently over-attended anchors.

Appendix D LeJEPA Mitigation Experiments: Training Details

We trained ViT-L models from scratch on ImageNet-1K for 100 epochs using the LeJEPA self-supervised objective [42], which combines a SIGReg regularization loss and a multi-view invariance loss. Architecture specifications are provided in Table 2, optimization hyperparameters in Table 3, regularization in Table 4, and data augmentation in Table 5. Each model was trained on 4 NVIDIA H100 GPUs using PyTorch DDP.

We evaluate six variants: (1) Baseline, (2) Registers (4 tokens), (3) Elementwise gating, (4) Elementwise gating + Registers, (5) Headwise gating, and (6) Headwise gating + Registers, each trained with three random seeds (9000, 9001, 9002). For results reported in Table 1, we select the better-performing gating variant (elementwise vs. headwise) based on mean ImageNet-1K linear probe accuracy across seeds; full per-seed linear probe results are provided in Table 6.

Compute resources.

Experiments were run on a compute cluster using NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The LeJEPA ViT-L experiments were trained with PyTorch DDP on 4 H100 GPUs per run; each 100-epoch run took approximately 3 days, corresponding to roughly 300 H100 GPU-hours per seed. We trained three seeds for each mitigation variant. The supervised ViT-L/16 gating+registers model was trained with PyTorch DDP on 4 H100 GPUs for 90 epochs for approximately 1 day, corresponding to roughly 100 H100 GPU-hours. Training linear semantic-segmentation probes on frozen LeJEPA backbones required one GPU per probe and only a few GPU-hours per probe. Similarly, toy-model experiments and pretrained-model diagnostics were run on a single GPU and were substantially cheaper than the LeJEPA training runs, typically completing within a few GPU-hours per run. All experiments were implemented in PyTorch.

Existing assets and licenses.

Table 8 lists the third-party datasets, codebases, and pretrained model checkpoints used in this work, together with their licenses or terms of use. We do not redistribute any third-party datasets or pretrained checkpoints.

Appendix E Additional Experimental Results and Figures

To produce the results in Figure 6 (right), we trained a ViT-L/16 with gating and registers from scratch on ImageNet-1k using supervised learning. The model was trained for 90 epochs using AdamW with a peak learning rate of 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} and an effective batch size of 512, achieving a top-1 validation accuracy of 76.18%.
